newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Euro airports aim to use more rail freight.
newsitem.headline: Euro airports aim to use more rail freight.

text.p: Three of continental Europe's largest airports are getting together to find ways to send more airfreight on Europe's rail network rather than by road.

Frits Bisschop, cargo director at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport told Reuters in an interview that Frankfurt and Schiphol, which had already been discussing the subject, have been approached by the managers of Paris's Charles de Gaulle.
"Paris CDG has clearly expressed its willingness to take part in this initiative. This month all three airport companies will sit together to see how to proceed," he stated.
"We aim to define the common requirements of the air cargo industry in respect of rail."
Frankfurt and Schiphol had already concluded that the air cargo industry is lacking an alternative to road transportation.
"There's more (road) congestion throughout Europe, and there's a need to find an answer to this," he said

"Rail may well be a better surface transport system than road, but so far, nothing has happened to effect a rail solution for the air freight sector. There have been many initiatives, many of which have failed and in many cases initiated by the railroad companies; and we have concluded that if you want to have a train service between, say, Frankfurt and Schiphol, then there's the need for some kind of standardisation: the only way to get that is to cooperate," he added."
All three airports could ultimately issue a tender to international railway companies defining their specific rail requirements.

"We could ask what sort of interface we would require between airports and railway, whether we will need combi (freight and passenger) trains or pure freight rail services, and who we would expect to handle airport rail terminal facilities," Bisschop said.
"Our belief is that if we have common agreement, we can tender to all railroad operators. I think working together as airports, we will create much more specific requirements."
"My personal feeling is that combi trains will be the route ahead. We know that when we talk about dedicated cargo trains you need volume and the air cargo business is not high volume."

"In the past there were initiatives which were looking for high volume air cargo, and we should look to reduce this dependence on high volume. I would prefer to have three times a day air freight wagons connected to a passenger train bound for Paris or Frankfurt," Bisschop stated.
A direct approach will ultimately be made to the European Union "I think we will also present the joint package to the European Union's Directorate General for Transport DG VII," he added.

"We would like to see if we can start a regular dialogue and we would like an update on their plans and policies as well as specific advice. Ultimately, in terms of finance, when we add detail to our research programme and perhaps find that certain modules of the programme policy fits in with EU goals, there may be a possibility for us to seek financial support for our plan," Bisschop said. - Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
